crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
children.blurb: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of producing legal answers, memos, and briefs where every claim is tied to a retrieved primary or secondary source, such as a case, statute, regulation, or treatise.

children.name: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
children.blurb: This page covers the use of AI systems to produce and test competing interpretations of statutes in litigation and regulatory disputes.

children.name: Brief Drafting with Machine Assistance
children.blurb: Brief drafting with machine assistance covers using language models and legal research tools to produce, revise, and check written submissions such as motions, memoranda, and appellate briefs.

children.name: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
children.blurb: Citation auditing and good law checking is the process of verifying that every authority cited in a legal document remains valid, has not been overruled or negatively treated, and still supports the proposition for which it is cited.

children.name: Jurisdictional Anomalies and Local Codes
children.blurb: Jurisdictional anomalies and local codes in AI law cover situations where state, municipal, or sector-specific rules diverge from federal or general principles, creating uneven obligations for developers and users.

sections.body: This field applies machine learning and language models to the practical work of finding law, reading statutes, drafting arguments, checking citations, and noticing local rules. Retrieval-grounded research means the system pulls from a fixed set of legal texts instead of generating from memory, so every claim can be traced to a source. Adversarial statutory reading asks the model to argue both sides of a provision, which helps a lawyer see weak points. Brief drafting with machine assistance produces structured first drafts, while citation auditing checks whether cited cases still say what the drafter claims. Jurisdictional anomalies and local codes covers the many small rules that differ by court or municipality.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Retrieval-grounded research is the most mature, because it depends on search and summarization rather than original legal reasoning. Citation auditing is also fairly reliable when it compares a quoted passage against a database of opinions, but it can miss changes in law that happened after the database was updated. Adversarial statutory interpretation is useful for surfacing arguments, yet it often produces plausible but wrong readings of complex statutes. Brief drafting can save time on structure and boilerplate, but the output still needs a lawyer to check every proposition. The honest limit is that none of these tools can replace a lawyer's judgment about strategy, risk, or what a particular judge will find persuasive. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows how quickly the legal environment around these tools is itself changing.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to understand how a model finds law should start with Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research, which explains the source-bound method behind the other pages. Adversarial Statutory Interpretation then shows how that retrieved text can be pushed and pulled to expose competing readings. Brief Drafting with Machine Assistance sits downstream, turning those readings into a first draft of an argument. Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking is the quality control step, verifying that the cases and statutes in that draft still support it. Jurisdictional Anomalies and Local Codes is the last check, because a brief that is correct in general may fail under a local rule or an unusual court practice. Together the pages move from finding law, to arguing it, to drafting it, to checking it, and finally to fitting it to a specific place.
